# GoodWolf Harness [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Python 3.12+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%2B-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)](#use-it-instructions-for-your-agent) [![Dependencies: standard library only](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-stdlib%20only-brightgreen.svg)](#use-it-instructions-for-your-agent) [![Claude Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude%20Code-supported-D97757?logo=claude&logoColor=white)](#where-it-stands) [![Codex](https://img.shields.io/badge/Codex-supported-412991?logo=openai&logoColor=white)](#where-it-stands) [![Cursor](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cursor-supported-000000?logo=cursor&logoColor=white)](#where-it-stands) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness)](https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness/commits/main) Project memory and a working method for coding agents. Every new session, a coding agent starts over knowing your code but not why it is the way it is, what is still undecided, or where yesterday's work stopped. Working with agents on one project for weeks hurts in three ways: - **The agent is ineffective.** It calls work done that doesn't work, or isn't what you meant. - **The agent is expensive.** Tokens, time and rework go on rediscovering what it already knew, and your attention goes on re-explaining it. - **You are in the wrong place.** Either decisions that matter get made without you, or you end up approving every step and babysitting work the agent could carry. GoodWolf answers all three from your repository: plain Markdown and a few standard-library Python scripts, in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. **Try it:** in your project, tell your coding agent *install the GoodWolf Harness from https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness*. It installs, then asks for your test commands and where it should stop for your yes. If your project already has a `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, the install stops and names the file: it doesn't move or merge them yet. Branch first, move them aside yourself, run the install again, and bring over what you need by hand. More under [Use it](#use-it-instructions-for-your-agent). ## What it does about each **So the work is what you meant, and it works:** - **What you decide gets built, and stays built.** A plan pulls the code toward it until the work matches. A decision about the architecture binds the code from then on: code that drifts from it is brought back, never the decision bent to fit the code, and it changes only when you decide again. - **Done means checked.** Each change becomes a ticket with checkable criteria and a written plan, is built test-first, and is verified against the ticket, the plan and your tests before it counts as done. - **Instructions that reach the agent.** Each rule lives in one place and is copied by a script to wherever it is read, and a check fails if a copy drifts. So the agent isn't working from scattered, contradictory instructions. **So you stop paying twice:** - **A memory of the project, not just of the code.** What was decided and why, what is half-built and at which step, and what is still undecided are kept as files. Every session starts from them, so "continue" is enough. - **Nothing you raise is lost.** Every open question is kept until it is answered, with where the thinking had got to, and the ones you keep returning to come up first. Each message is placed under the question it is about, so a side remark is noted instead of derailing the work. **So you are where it matters, and nowhere else:** - **Decisions go by their weight.** A decision whose mistake would break several parts of the project comes to you, with the agent's recommendation. Anything smaller the agent settles and tells you about. When it is unsure which one it is, it asks. - **You set the stops.** Commit, push, starting the next piece of work, splitting work into tickets: each is `ask` or `auto`. Out of the box, everything asks. - **You can see what it stands on.** Every step leaves a short record you can read, so checking the agent's work is cheap and trusting it isn't blind. - **You can think out loud.** Jump from topic to topic. What you say lands under the question it belongs to and comes back when that topic does. **Two goals it can't promise yet:** - **Better over time, not worse.** One home for every decision, a maintenance pass that keeps documents and code in agreement, and rules reworded each time the agent ignores one all point this way. Nothing yet measures whether it holds. - **No harm.** The harness's own scripts refuse rather than overwrite, and push waits for your yes. Nothing yet bounds what the agent itself may do. ## A morning with it An illustration: the project is made up; the steps are what the harness does. **You:** continue **Agent:** Picking up from yesterday. The export endpoint landed, but one of its acceptance checks is still open: the CSV header test was never written. Next in the queue is the import endpoint. And your question from Tuesday — do retries need idempotency keys? — is still open; we were leaning yes. Close out the export first? **You:** Yes, then import. *It writes the test, ticks the check, and plans the import. Halfway through, it stops.* **Agent:** `docs/architecture.md` doesn't say whether an import is all-or-nothing or row by row. I'd go all-or-nothing: a half-applied import is hard to undo. Your call? **You:** All-or-nothing. **Agent:** Added to `docs/architecture.md`, with the reason. *It builds the import test-first, runs your tests, checks the result against the ticket, and asks before committing.* **You:** Oh — exports will need paging at some point. **Agent:** Noted as an open question under exports. It will come up again when you next work on exports. *Two days later, a fresh session:* **You:** Let's make imports row by row, it's simpler. **Agent:** Two days ago we settled on all-or-nothing, because a half-applied import is hard to undo. Has something changed? If so, I'll reopen it and record why. You don't type the steps or learn the commands. The agent moves the work along and stops wherever you have told it to ask. ## Who it is for, and what it costs It is for **steering agents on a project that lives for months**, in one session or several at once — a long-lived product, a large refactor, a codebase you return to between other work — where forgetting costs more every week. It is not worth it in a prototype's first week, when there is nothing settled yet to keep, or for one-off scripts. Before you install, know this: - **Several sessions at once, yes; keeping them apart is your host's job.** Sessions in one tree see where the others stand, and the harness's own scripts refuse a write to an entry that moved since it was read. Nothing here locks a file: that is your host's — its edit tool refuses to write over a file that changed since the agent read it, and where it offers a worktree per session, each works in its own. A team sharing one queue across branches is not tested yet, and your team's tracker can't yet take the tickets' place. - **No fast path for small work yet.** Every change is meant to go through ticket, plan, build and verify. You can tell the agent to skip that for a one-line fix, but nothing yet says when that is fine. - **Instructions, not enforcement.** Everything here is the agent following written rules, plus scripts that check the files. A model can still slip; the records make the slip visible, and the rule it missed gets reworded. - **No uninstall command.** Everything it adds is files, so reverting the install commit removes the harness. What it wrote under `docs/` afterwards stays until you delete it. What it saves has not been measured. To judge it, install it into one project and watch three things over a few weeks: whether an agent arriving cold re-decides less of what was settled, whether work survives the end of a session without you reconstructing it, and whether drift between documents and code falls rather than documents piling up. ## It changes with your project Rule files for agents rot. Rules pile up and contradict each other, the agent quietly ignores some, and your edits get overwritten when you pull an update. Here: - **Your changes survive updates.** Your test commands, your approval settings, and any shipped rule you want different go in one file, `local.rules.md`. Every install and update applies it last and never touches it. If you edited a shipped file by hand instead, an update stops and tells you rather than overwrite it. - **A rule the agent ignored gets reworded, and the next miss shows whether that worked.** When a rule was in place and not followed, the agent logs the miss in `docs/rule-failures.md`, shows you the rewording, and lands it as one commit you can review and revert. So far it is you who notices the miss: every one in this repository's log was caught by the person, not the agent. - **No two copies of a rule disagree.** Each rule is written in one place and copied by a script into every instruction that uses it. A check fails if a copy drifts from its source; it runs at every install and update, and in your own checks if you add it there. - **Your own skills get the same checks.** A guided command, `/mechanism`, walks you through adding one, and the scripts that check the shipped skills then check yours. - **Anything provisional says what it waits on.** A rule that will change once an open question is answered names that question, and the session report tells you when the answer has landed. **An example from this repository's log.** One rule tells the agent to file each of your messages under the open question it belongs to. On 5 October, new sessions kept filing messages under questions that only sounded similar. Each time, the miss was logged and the rule tightened — four times that day — until it said: file a message under the narrowest question that actually covers it, never under one that merely looks alike. The sessions after that got it right. The harness has been built with itself for over a month, in 57 sessions, and its log holds 41 misses so far. To override a shipped rule, add a section naming it. ## How it works **When a document and the code disagree, which one is fixed.** Every written thing in the project is one of four kinds, and the kind says which side wins. | the document says | who is right | when they disagree | for example | |---|---|---|---| | what it intends to become | the document, until the code gets there | the code moves toward it; the document is done once they match | a ticket, a plan, an open question | | what must always hold | the document, always | the code is fixed; the document changes only by a decision | the architecture, the glossary | | what exists | the code | the document is rebuilt from the code, never edited by hand | the ticket list, a check's report | | what happened | neither — it is past | nothing is fixed | a session record, a finished ticket | **How the right things reach the agent.** There is no vector database and no similarity search; what the agent reads is chosen by which question you are on. Open questions form a tree, each under the one it is part of. When a session starts, the agent reads a status report: the open questions you keep returning to, the ones parked until a condition that may now hold, and what other running sessions are on. Before each reply it reads the part of the tree around the question you are on, and follows links from there. **The steps.** You won't type these; they are the names you will see in the agent's replies. A session starts with `/recall`, which finds where the work stopped; `/align` settles with you whatever needs deciding; `/conclude` writes down what the next session needs. A piece of work moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` → `/verify` → `/maintain`; large work is first agreed with you on its question and split into small tickets. `/verify` asks whether finished work keeps the promises its ticket and plan made; `/maintain` asks whether the documents still agree with each other and with the code. - Installing into a project, updating it, and checking that the installed copy is intact, with
  your own rules applied last.
- Arriving in a project that already has code: the first session after install works out with
  you what the project is, and writes its architecture, decisions and glossary from that
  conversation, deepening as the work reaches each part.
- The open-question tree, with every message placed in it before the reply.
- Each rule kept in one place, and checks on the harness's own files, run at install and update.

**Not yet:**

- <straw-dog question="q-0037.0013.0002">You can't yet say which kinds of decision stop for you; the line between yours and the agent's is drawn by its judgement of what bears load.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0011.0004">The install doesn't yet find what your project exists to solve, or the answers already built into its docs and code; the first session builds them with you instead.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0020.0002.0003">Updates name the files they changed, not what changed in them or what your project has to do about it.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0018">There is no way yet to send improvements your project makes to the harness back upstream.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0023">Other hosts — Copilot, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and the rest — aren't supported yet.</straw-dog>

## Use it (instructions for your agent)

Asked to install the harness into a project:

1. Clone this repository beside the project, never into it. Already cloned into the folder where
   the project was meant to be? From that folder,
   `python .agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --install --replace-clone` turns the clean clone into
   an install; go on to step 3.
2. From the project's root, run `python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --install`. It
   writes nothing if it refuses, and says why.
3. Read [`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md`](.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md) and follow it: it
   says how to report what arrived and how to set up the project's own rules with the person.
   Updating and checking the installed copy are in the same skill.

What lands in your repository: `.agents/` (the skills, the scripts and their tests), `AGENTS.md`
(the rules every session reads), a one-line `CLAUDE.md` pointing to it, and a starting work queue
in `docs/tickets/`. `local.rules.md` and the rest of `docs/` — architecture, decisions, questions,
session notes — are written as you work. Claude Code and Cursor reach the skills through symbolic
links the install makes in each clone; on Windows, where creating one may need an elevated
prompt, it prints the command to run.

Python 3.12 or later, standard library only. [MIT licensed](LICENSE).

terms — *commit on main and push each commit, or keep my
work on a branch of its own*, never as a setting's name, the origin's own answers offered
as no default; the links the platform refused, as the commands to run. End with the first question

92	**Q1** Before drafting a reply, say what the turn is, reading this turn's window — the one the host's
93	hook put in your context, or `questions.py --window --session <tag>`, the script being
94	`.agents/scripts/gw/questions.py`:
95	
96	- **On a question**: call `at` on the lowest question that contains the message. One that only
97	  resembles it is not its home; from a question that does not contain it, go up. Going up past
98	  two or more questions that resemble the message, their parent is not its home either: the
99	  question they jointly serve is missing — read the questions skill and open it, or the turn is

101	  under it.
102	- **A new question**: the question the message is one case of, worded as the store would hold it.
103	  Look for its answer in the docs and the code first — found, point to it and open nothing for
104	  it; the turn is on the question that contains it, placed as above — a missing parent is still
105	  opened. Not found, or what the answer leaves unsettled, `open` it under the lowest question
106	  that contains it, and call `at` on it.

108	  on that question.
109	- **Uncharted**, a question whose home you cannot settle: no call. Ask the user where it belongs,
110	  in every reply until answered.
111	- **Banter**, a message that asks nothing of the work — no question about the project, nothing
112	  to do or decide: no call. Answer it. The reply writes nothing and settles nothing; a doubt, or
113	  an answer that would do either, makes the turn another kind.
114	
115	The calls:
116	
117	- `questions.py at q-0004 --session <tag>`
118	- `questions.py open '<question>' --under q-0004 --session <tag>`, which prints the id it gave
119	- `questions.py close q-0004 decided '[link](../path.md) — who, date' --session <tag>`
120	
121	The store's other calls are made whenever the turn's own work settles, opens or moves a question.
122	Only the working agent calls, never a helper. For any other call, a closure, a branching or a
123	drop, read the questions skill.
124	
125	**Q5** Every time a reply names a question — a table's cell included — its whole id is a link to its
126	entry; the first time, its question follows as the window writes it, save where a table's form
127	names it by its id alone. No word stands in for a question a reader has not been shown — *as
128	before*, *the same* — it is named. A question the store does not hold yet is written out, never
129	named after the ticket it will belong to.
130	</installed>
131	
132	## Core and instance
133	
134	`docs/` is substituted whole in a harness instance: a recipient project replaces its contents with
135	its own.
136	
137	What core may not do is **depend** on it. Nothing under `.agents/` may reference a file in `docs/`,
138	or rely on one for its instruction or for any separable part of its own functioning. A core file
139	may name a path under `docs/` only when that path is a record a mechanism declares — the directory
140	that holds a kind of record, or a file that is one — never a particular record inside such a
141	directory: `docs/tickets/` and `docs/glossary.md` are painted doors; one particular ticket inside
142	`docs/tickets/` is a document only this project has. Content inside the
143	[local block](#project-local) is the instance's, not core's. A `<straw-dog>` exempts
144	nothing: its wrapper is stripped on install and whatever it wrapped ships. Core names a particular
145	record of this tree only in a straw dog's binding, and that record is a question; it names no
146	ticket anywhere — in a link or as a bare id in prose — since a recipient can resolve neither.
147	
148	## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest
149	
150	A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
151	- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
152	- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
153	- Load-bearing — see the definition below
154	
155	A decision forms in the body of the question it answers and lands in one of these as it is made —
156	as a straw dog while an open question's answer can still change it. A decision about a
157	mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.
158	
159	Bad architectural documentation:
160	- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.
161	
162	Better:
163	- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
164	
165	## What makes a thing "load-bearing"
166	
167	- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
168	- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
169	is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.
170	
171	- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.
172	
173	## The loop
174	
175	Two rings, joined at /align.
176	
177	    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
178	    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket
179	
180	/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
181	a load-bearing shape is aligned on its question until its `Where it stands` is accepted, /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.
182	
183	Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; a question's `Where it stands` accepted; and
184	whatever stands at or above its ladder's dial under [Autonomy](#autonomy).
185	
186	Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.
187	
188	### Helpers
189	
190	- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (an align on its question for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
191	- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.
192	
193	## Self-improvement
194	
195	- A rule that was in place and did not fire was usually worded wrong. Register the failure in docs/rule-failures.md, or strike the entry it repeats, and propose the amendment that would have made it fire; /mechanism and /skill-up hold the means. Land the amendment in the same pass, showing its text first.
196	- A slip no rule covers is registered there too, described broadly enough to recognise its repeat;
197	  one proposes no rule.
198	- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
199	
200	## Autonomy
201	
202	Autonomy is a dial on a ladder. A method whose decisions differ in how far their consequences
203	reach has a ladder, its rungs ordered by that reach and declared by the method's mechanism; a
204	method without one states which of its decisions are the agent's and which the person's. A
205	decision's rung is read from what it decides, never from the record that holds it; a case between
206	two rungs takes the higher.
207	
208	- 🤖 Below the dial the agent settles and acts on its own.
209	- ✋ At the dial it settles, and shows the person before acting.
210	- 💬 Above it, it settles nothing: it brings the options and a recommendation, and the person
211	  decides.
212	
213	A question carries its highest rung on each ladder it touches and stops for the person while that
214	rung is at or above the ladder's dial. Mending a violation is the work of the rung the mended thing
215	is on. Work closes with its commit once `/verify` passes on it; a push follows the project's way of
216	working with git, as its local file states.
217	
218	The project sets each dial in its local block; an unset dial is at the lowest rung. The agent never
219	writes its dial, and the host refuses an edit that changes it.
220	
221	Development's ladder, lowest first:
222	
223	| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
224	|---|---|
225	| code | writing the code inside agreed work |
226	| a feature | what one piece of work should deliver |
227	| load-bearing | a load-bearing architectural decision, e.g. module boundaries |
228	| a product slice | what gets built next |
229	| the whole product | what the project is for |
230	
231	An install proposes the dial at *a feature*.
232	
233	Self-improvement's ladder, lowest first:
234	
235	| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
236	|---|---|
237	| a wording | rewording an instruction, its meaning unchanged |
238	| a script | fixing a script that carries an instruction out |
239	| a rule | changing an instruction or a skill |
240	| the method | changing the way of working |
241	
242	An install proposes the dial at *a rule*.
243	
244	## Project-local
245	
246	<installed by="mechanism-shape">
247	**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
248	`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
249	installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
250	there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
251	overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
252	file, and re-installed. The local block is the project's,
253	not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
254	</installed>
255	
256	## Straw dogs
257	
258	Wrap anything an open question's answer will change, as you write it — or, for text already
259	written, in the pass that opens the question: `<straw-dog question="q-N">`, bound to the question
260	whose answer will rewrite it, or in code a `TODO` naming `q-N` first. Treat *not yet*, *until*,
261	*once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find the question, or
262	open one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it. Write the body
263	to stand on its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it names no
264	question or ticket — the binding does. Leave what no open question would change unwrapped.
265	
266	Follow a straw dog like any other rule until it is due, as the listing and the wake report; then
267	act on reality, rewrite it to what is now true, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

- `questions.py open '<question>' --under q-0004 --session <tag>`, which prints the id it gave

entry; the first time, its question follows as the window writes it, save where a table's form
names it by its id alone. No word stands in for a question a reader has not been shown — *as
before*, *the same* — it is named. A question the store does not hold yet is written out, never
named after the ticket it will belong to.
</installed>

## Core and instance

`docs/` is substituted whole in a harness instance: a recipient project replaces its contents with
its own.

What core may not do is **depend** on it. Nothing under `.agents/` may reference a file in `docs/`,
or rely on one for its instruction or for any separable part of its own functioning. A core file
may name a path under `docs/` only when that path is a record a mechanism declares — the directory
that holds a kind of record, or a file that is one — never a particular record inside such a
directory: `docs/tickets/` and `docs/glossary.md` are painted doors; one particular ticket inside
`docs/tickets/` is a document only this project has. Content inside the
[local block](#project-local) is the instance's, not core's. A `<straw-dog>` exempts
nothing: its wrapper is stripped on install and whatever it wrapped ships. Core names a particular
record of this tree only in a straw dog's binding, and that record is a question; it names no
ticket anywhere — in a link or as a bare id in prose — since a recipient can resolve neither.

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in the body of the question it answers and lands in one of these as it is made —
as a straw dog while an open question's answer can still change it. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.

Bad architectural documentation:
- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
a load-bearing shape is aligned on its question until its `Where it stands` is accepted, /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; a question's `Where it stands` accepted; and
whatever stands at or above its ladder's dial under [Autonomy](#autonomy).

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (an align on its question for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.

## Self-improvement

- A rule that was in place and did not fire was usually worded wrong. Register the failure in docs/rule-failures.md, or strike the entry it repeats, and propose the amendment that would have made it fire; /mechanism and /skill-up hold the means. Land the amendment in the same pass, showing its text first.
- A slip no rule covers is registered there too, described broadly enough to recognise its repeat;
  one proposes no rule.
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.

## Autonomy

Autonomy is a dial on a ladder. A method whose decisions differ in how far their consequences
reach has a ladder, its rungs ordered by that reach and declared by the method's mechanism; a
method without one states which of its decisions are the agent's and which the person's. A
decision's rung is read from what it decides, never from the record that holds it; a case between
two rungs takes the higher.

- 🤖 Below the dial the agent settles and acts on its own.
- ✋ At the dial it settles, and shows the person before acting.
- 💬 Above it, it settles nothing: it brings the options and a recommendation, and the person
  decides.

A question carries its highest rung on each ladder it touches and stops for the person while that
rung is at or above the ladder's dial. Mending a violation is the work of the rung the mended thing
is on. Work closes with its commit once `/verify` passes on it; a push follows the project's way of
working with git, as its local file states.

The project sets each dial in its local block; an unset dial is at the lowest rung. The agent never
writes its dial, and the host refuses an edit that changes it.

Development's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| code | writing the code inside agreed work |
| a feature | what one piece of work should deliver |
| load-bearing | a load-bearing architectural decision, e.g. module boundaries |
| a product slice | what gets built next |
| the whole product | what the project is for |

An install proposes the dial at *a feature*.

Self-improvement's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| a wording | rewording an instruction, its meaning unchanged |
| a script | fixing a script that carries an instruction out |
| a rule | changing an instruction or a skill |
| the method | changing the way of working |

An install proposes the dial at *a rule*.

## Project-local

<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
file, and re-installed. The local block is the project's,
not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
</installed>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything an open question's answer will change, as you write it — or, for text already
written, in the pass that opens the question: `<straw-dog question="q-N">`, bound to the question
whose answer will rewrite it, or in code a `TODO` naming `q-N` first. Treat *not yet*, *until*,
*once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find the question, or
open one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it. Write the body
to stand on its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it names no
question or ticket — the binding does. Leave what no open question would change unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until it is due, as the listing and the wake report; then
act on reality, rewrite it to what is now true, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

GoodWolf Harness установлен в `codename_japaka`. Папка была пустой, поэтому установщик сам сделал здесь `git init`. Установку я закоммитил (`f07af78`), проверка целостности проходит.

Что он даёт. Каждая работа становится тикетом с критериями, и готовой она считается только после проверки по этим критериям. Решения, открытые вопросы и место, где остановилась работа, хранятся в `docs/`. Поэтому новой сессии достаточно сказать «continue», и ничего не придётся объяснять заново. Вы решаете только то, что выше выбранного вами порога, а ниже него агент действует сам.

Я написал [local.rules.md](local.rules.md) с настройками проекта:
- **Описание проекта.** Пока это просто «пустой проект». Для чего он, решим вместе в первой сессии.
- **Запуск Python.** Здесь он запускается через `py -3`, потому что `python` в PATH нет.
- **Проверки.** Своих тестов у проекта ещё нет, поэтому пока проверяются только записи самого harness. Когда появится код, добавим сюда его тесты.

Чтобы всё заработало, осталось три вещи, по одной за раз.

**1. Ссылки на навыки для Claude Code и Cursor.** Windows не дал их создать без прав администратора. Выполните в **cmd от имени администратора** (команда `mklink` есть только в cmd, в PowerShell её нет):

```bash
mklink /D "D:\Dev\AI\codename_japaka\.claude\skills" "..\.agents\skills"
```

```bash
mklink /D "D:\Dev\AI\codename_japaka\.cursor\skills" "..\.agents\skills"
```

Вторая нужна, только если вы работаете в Cursor. Скажите, когда выполните, и я проверю, что ссылки работают.

**2. Где я останавливаюсь и жду вашего «да».** Начнём с разработки. Уровни решений, от мелких к крупным:

1. 🤖 код внутри уже согласованной работы
2. ✋ что должна дать отдельная функция (по умолчанию порог здесь)
3. 💬 несущие архитектурные решения, например границы модулей
4. 💬 что строим следующим
5. 💬 для чего вообще проект

🤖 значит, что я делаю сам. ✋ значит, что я решаю, но показываю вам перед тем, как действовать. 💬 значит, что я приношу варианты и рекомендацию, а решаете вы. Оставить порог на строке 2 или назначить другую?

После этого спрошу про порог для изменения правил самого harness и про то, как вы работаете с git: коммитить в main и сразу пушить или держать работу в отдельной ветке.
